translations.text: Causes are what set speech in motion, and speech is what tells of causes. For this reason they first come to the senses, and the senses deliver them to the faculty that receives them,

and the receiving faculty passes them to the one that judges, and the judging faculty to the one that keeps them. In this way the thing that has taken shape turns back, is breathed into the pipe of its own tongue, and sounds forth in an ordered way,
so that through this shared hearing it may in turn pass to the hearing of others. This is our present undertaking.
For it is right to make known what the blessed ones have reported, the writing of those recorded by hand [?], as an account of those great men,
who ought to be spread abroad as preaching to the whole world by the ministers of the word, through revelation from on high, and who were made glorious by the revelation of the truth.
We are not looking for something that is easily drawn up. Rather, we wish to bring clearly to light precious pearls from the depths of the sea, which can only be won with labour,
and which are ready to be shared out as wealth, the incorruptible treasure of divine gifts, among our people, through the word of grace.
Brother Michael, I have read the letter with your request. I understood how eager your request was, and your love of learning pleased me greatly,
for you wished me to write the Life of the great John of Zedazeni and send it to your desert. First,
you wished it so that the virtues of that holy father and teacher would not stay hidden in the depths. Second, you wished it so that we might gain benefit from them.
There was also the small sheet of writing you sent us. From it I read about the deeds of our father of Zedazeni, and we gathered some further information about him and his disciples
and about the places connected with them. You were like someone who sends grains of gold to a craftsman so that he may gather them together and make them into a beautiful vessel.
With this eagerness of yours, you are not receiving anything from us. Instead you are giving to me. It is like the Lord of glory when he came to the well and asked the Samaritan woman for water:
he was not receiving but was bestowing the spring of life. In the same way I am the one who receives, not the one who gives to you.
As for me, when I saw the good guest who had come to me, I ran out with joy and brought him up into my room, and I want to satisfy the hunger that brought him seeking.
But when I opened my treasury, I found it lacking and small because of my limited knowledge. I stammer and cannot speak well, so where am I to begin telling the virtues of this holy man!
But I decided to imitate the hard-working bee and gather flowers from the beautiful gardens of books, so that
I may prepare sweet food for those who long for it, to our praise. But first it is right that we send prayer ahead [?]. Join hands with me in supplication!
For prayer is what makes all good things fragrant. Prayer nourished Samuel in his mother's womb and revealed him as a prophet.
See the fruit of prayer: he became a prophet of truth from his childhood, because Hannah asked for him with tears and prayer.
Again, when Moses the lawgiver was to bring [?] the tablets of the Law, he made forty days of prayer and fasting their foundation. And the tablets of Moses, written by the finger of God,
he brought down from the mountain once, and then a second time to complete the work. The first tablets were broken as being Jewish [?], but the second were honoured by the change.
Therefore it is fitting that everyone who undertakes divine service should ask of him who is God, the generous bestower, and he will give nourishment, as James the apostle says:
"If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask, and God, the distributor of gifts, will give it to him."
At the beginning of the writers it is fitting to make mention of the great Moses, who began the writing of the house [?], the foreshadower of the truth,
he who, like Noah's ark, was carried on the water, armed [or: enclosed] by glory, cast away out of fear,
was rescued by the providence of God [lit. 'of gods'; ?]. He was raised by Pharaoh's daughter in the very house of that same king, and he killed the Egyptian,
the son-in-law of Pharaoh, who was not distant and hidden but close to Pharaoh, since he was a type of all the truth,
the first one: that son-in-law of Pharaoh of the new law [?], of the Pharaoh of the bodiless Pharaoh [?], as Egypt is of hell, the two being close to each other in figure.
He fled from the wrath of the king and went out into the desert, to Mount Sinai.
The angel of God appeared to him in fire within the bush (the mystery of the Virgin!), and, struck with awe, he came to see.
He was called by him, stripped the skin of the dead from his living feet, and presented himself for the revelation,
he who, from that same Most High, was confessed [or: believed] to be the God of Pharaoh [?], of the prince of darkness, the apostate from the supreme good [?], he
who became higher than the loftiest summits of the mountains (the type of the true lawgiver!). Him he sent with wonders and signs to deliver Israel.
But the one who sent him revealed himself to him, who he was, and said:
"I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob, and of the one who made [it] known to your fathers [?].
He made his name known through the mountain [?] to the three patriarchs, great [?] and righteous; he was named God. Then Moses, the receiver, again asks God:
"If they say to me, 'Who sent you?', what shall I say?" The One taught him to speak a depth out of the abyss, and said to him: "Say this to them: He who is has sent me."
He is the One Who Is, who has no beginning. And as confirmation he gave him the ten very great wonders, by which he is the God of the fathers,
so that they might believe in the boundary of the knowledge of the true God, that great light. Darkness and the deep seized them, and they were swallowed up.
And that which is the light is the one invisible and unchangeable God, without beginning and without end, immeasurable,
ever blessed, the light of the Trinity, for this unites the three persons of the most divine [?]: together with Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
Thus it is reckoned as united, without confusion and without division, and it is not right to make the Son less than the Father, nor the Spirit less than the Son.
And if the Godhead were not so, it would not be greatly glorified; for he is invisible, timeless, uncontainable, unchangeable, unchangeable without quality,
without quantity or form, incomprehensible and indivisible. He moves himself eternally and mightily, with a motion of his own, even though everything tends toward the first cause,
which is his, as the Son, the only one who is living and life-giving, the giver of life, as he says:
"I am living, and you too shall live, and whoever believes in me shall also live through me."
That Light, ever-blessed and radiant, not separate from the most exalted nature of being, Light eternal [?].
And the Holy Spirit is the Lord of sovereignty. He sends forth and he apportions, and he makes a person his own temple, as he wills and in whomever he wills.
For the Spirit is the giver and creator, and is not created. By him was established also that created light of the secondary radiances, I mean of the angels,
and the third light, this heaven. These had their beginning from that first light, the light of the origin [?], from which are three, and from the three one. But only this:

the Father is not the Son, and the Son is not the Father, and the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son. This does not divide the nature. Rather, it makes a distinction within the nature and points to unity.
But those who have not understood the equality of the Trinity are in darkness and [?]. Let them be ashamed of Arius,
who dared to call the Word of God created, the Word that was his own and not another's.
And this happened to him because he did not understand the boundary between his person and his nature. He saw him as a man and did not recognize the nature of the Godhead, which is without beginning.
And again there are the Arians, who say of Christ that he was the Word of God, and who again joined the Spirit to the created things, and say that God created the Word as he created Adam.
For [?], you most senseless of all men: if it was his Word, how could part of his Godhead be without beginning and part be created?
Whatever a builder makes, whether a pillar or a temple, is not called the builder's word, but something made by a word.
So how could Christ be the Word of God and that Word also be created?! Their own [words] condemn them!
If the Word was not with him, did the one without beginning create it afterwards?! Then by your own word God was wordless before that!
And again one should reply to the questioner, to all those who do not accept the equality of the Holy Trinity: is God receptive of accident, or not?
If he admits that God is not receptive of accident, let us ask: is the Word of God an accident, or not?
If he says that it is an accident, I would be denying what I have confessed.
But far be it that anything should have entered into God that was not there before, for then he would appear to be receptive of it.
For everything that is receptive can be increased and diminished. How is it possible to say of God that he is increased and diminished?
It remains, then, that it is substance [?], for everything is divided into these two: substance [?] and accident.
And whatever was not an accident is clearly substance [?], and whatever is substance [?] subsists by itself.
And what belongs to God is creator and not created. I mean the Word without beginning, through whom God created every created thing.
And it cannot be otherwise, for everything is divided into two kinds: created and creator.
And that which is creator, and is created [?]. It is evident that the Word is not created. To put it briefly, there is nothing among created things that could be a creator.
I say the same of the Holy Spirit as well. But Macedonius dared to count the Holy Spirit among the created things,
and [to speak of] the coming of that sovereign Holy Spirit as by grace. That bold and arrogant man thought himself to be something he was not.
This man strengthened his tongue to fight against God, even after hearing that fearful saying:
"All sins and blasphemies will be forgiven to men, but blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven."
Nor did he understand that saying of the prophet David:
"By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their host."
If he is the Spirit of his mouth, how could the Holy Spirit be created!
For everything that exists is his. If the Spirit were created, then the Father would have been without a Spirit until that Spirit was created!
Rather, its Creator is that Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father and is worshipped together with the Son,
that Spirit who moved upon the waters, and by that moving over them gave form to and created all created things, and by grace brought forth each one as he willed;
that Spirit who came down like fire upon the apostles and, with a most surpassing wonder, divided the tongues.
Behold, a grace beyond words: the apostle speaks in Hebrew, in one tongue only, and all the barbarians hear him in every tongue!
From this Spirit may the spirit of wisdom, knowledge and understanding come upon us, and may the grace of speech be given to our tongue to find words,
so that I may speak without error about the holy John of Zedazeni, to praise him, for the benefit of the [?] (spodioni) of the deserts, who are zealous.
And you, prepare your ears and receive this with faith. Do not expect to hear all the virtue of that man, but only a little out of much, because it would take so long to tell.
This blessed John came from the land of Mesopotamia, and under the guidance of the Holy Spirit he came to the land of Kartli,
near this our mother-city of Mtskheta. He had devoted himself to Christ from his childhood.
He took up the heavy yoke from his youth, sat alone and kept silence, for there is hope in endurance.
He first began the monastic life in his own land, in Assyria.
He lived in all humility, and through fasting and vigil, tears and supplication, labor and patience, he advanced day by day,
so that he might attain the perfection he would receive, of which it says: "Knock and it will be opened to you; seek and you will find."
Once he was enlightened, he first reached that glory. He saw what was far away as if it were near, and he shone like a star,
and the mighty works multiplied that were done through him by God: healings of many kinds of disease, and the casting out of demons.
Then he left the place where he lived and went into a remote desert. There he found a cave and settled in it with his disciples,
and for a long time no one knew of that place. Only rarely did he send one of his disciples out to fetch food.
So he lived there in secret, thinking he was hiding himself.
But God again revealed his servant, for this is God's custom:
everyone who humbles himself will be exalted. People began to come to him again, even there,
…who was hidden in the cave. People brought the sick there on litters, afflicted in all kinds of ways, and there they found relief.
Why do I say this? It is not to tell you, brethren, about some of his deeds and his life there. Rather, I am telling you the reason he came to this land of ours.
For the earlier life and deeds of this blessed man are written in the first book, and it is blessed [?] for us to write them down a second time.
Then the blessed John began to consider in his mind that he should go away to a distant land,
where there was no report at all of his virtues to be heard. And he kept saying: "Where shall I take heed [?], so that it may be right for his journey to prosper?"
But while he was only thinking it over, his guide, the Holy Spirit, pointed him to the northern land, in order to lead him to the land of Kartli.
For there is one who wishes to set out from here [?], but someone else was the one who brought him: the one who once called Abraham and said to him:
"Go out from your land and from among your kindred, and go to the land that I will show you."
From one land and from one lineage he brought forth Abraham and John;
for truly holy John was of the offspring of Abraham. Hear what the apostle Paul says:
"If you are Christ's, then you are indeed Abraham's children, heirs according to the promise." Truly the holy root brought forth good [fruit].
Then the blessed John began to consider it and said to his disciples: "Stay here, for I want to go away to a distant land, in case I find what I am seeking."
And the saying of the prophet Elisha calls the blessed disciples to mind:
"As the Lord lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you alone as long as you go on."
We drink from that spring every day and are filled by it. Let us not deprive ourselves of it in these few days of ours.
And whatever you have seen to be good for yourself, consider it pleasing for us as well."
O, the good harmony of the disciples of that fair teacher! They were bound together by the bond of love, and together they were drawn toward the [?] of Christ.
Then he set out from his own land for the land of Kartli. He was guided by that invisible power which once, in the form of a star, led the Magi.
He arrived at this capital city of ours, Mtskheta. After he had venerated the holy churches, he went in before the holy Catholic Pillar.
This pillar was raised up by God and revealed from above with great wonder. For a long time it was held up in the air above the doors [?], and all the people of Kartli saw it.
God, not man, made it firm, so that its foundations would stay unshaken forever.
News of it spread through every land. For three days, all the efforts of craftsmen and kings, with a countless multitude, could not raise it.
They used up all their strength. Then they gave up and went away in the evening, taking all their machines with them, and all hope was lost.

That same night, the cause of all the good things of Kartli, our holy and flourishing mother Nino, remained in prayer with tears. With every kind of supplication she asked for help from Christ, our mighty God, and quickly took it captive [?].
And that captive [?] … to all the power of the king and the skill of the craftsmen [?].
By prayer she received that living pillar, and it hung up in the air, raised one cubit above its base and standing upright.
And when dawn broke, behold, King Mirian and all the multitude of Kartli arrived and saw that great wonder, the mystery from God, which was done for their salvation.
And it came down slowly, a little at a time, until it was set firm on the base prepared for it. Everyone was astonished, and they marvelled at that great faith.
They glorified the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and the renewal of faith grew greatly among those believers.
From then on the other pillars were raised, and they built the church, of which the apostle Paul makes mention:
"How one ought to behave in the house of God, which is the church, the pillar and foundation of the truth, which was shown to angels, was preached among the Gentiles, and was believed in the world."
Holy John hastened to this pillar clothed in light, as to a place that God had wondrously revealed and that was held in honour.
He prayed to God. He lifted up his eyes, raised his hands and shed his precious tears before the pillar of the living Son, so that He would show him the place where he should complete his course.

Then He who does the will of those who fear Him soon showed them this mountain near Mtskheta, to the east, north of the life-giving Cross, so that he would go up to the summit of that mountain and dwell there.
And as he set out, he crossed the river Aragvi. He came before the Cross, the giver of life,
under whose wings it shelters everyone from every evil happening: the light revealed from on high through a great wonder, the light confirmed by God.
And he prayed for a long time. Then he went out from there and climbed the high mountain called Zedazadeni, where his monastery is now built.
For that place was entirely wooded. And when he saw it, it pleased him, and he said:
"This is my place of rest; here, then, I will dwell, for I have desired it. I will bless its wild beasts with a blessing."
But as I think, O blessed one, this saying is yours: "Who would give me wings like a dove's? I would fly away, I would rise up on high, I would go and find rest in the wilderness."
For the Lord settled him here for two reasons:
First, so that he and his disciples would become the ornament and crown of this city of ours, like those twelve stones, honoured to look upon, set in the tunic of Aaron;
a benefit and a healer for all who live in this city of ours and call upon them, as will be told to you a little later.
And second, because the place to which he was sent had been a tower of the former nobles, where idol-worship had been exalted,
and the devil was served by them with the smoke of their offerings. So the service of God was to be exalted in those very places,
and the poison of those wicked demons was to be purged from there, as Sabbas once did at the place called Castellion.
The hosts of demons were driven away. That blessed elder prayed, and they pray to God at all times and stand undisturbed.
He endured all the attacks of the devil, and he entrusted himself to prayer and fasting, as to the mother of wisdom.
Our holy father John wished to live alone. He longed for his own dwelling place, that city whose architect and maker is God,
the heavenly Jerusalem. As a seeker of the heavenly pearl, he longed to join the good merchants in their festival of delight.
Here he put himself to death so that he might find eternal life.
Then one day that good teacher called his disciples and said to them: "Why do you stand idle?
Do you not know that the Lord our God Jesus Christ sent us out for the benefit of this land? The people of this world are a new planting.
It is right for each of you to go out and strengthen the brethren
who have confessed Christ our Lord. Do this not by the words of your teaching, but so that you may also present yourselves as an example.
This is why the Lord has left us among the gentiles early, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven.
Brethren, let nothing be dearer to you than God. Despise the love of silver and riches. Do not give yourselves over to luxury, gluttony, and food,
for luxury and food gave birth to Adam's disobedience, which has rested upon his offspring. It was this that drove him out of the paradise of delights.
If that law of fasting had been kept, this thorny earth would not have been given to us, and death would not have ruled over us. Yet that Power from on high humbled itself:
he took flesh. Through him we attained that first desire of ours, something higher than paradise. We took from the tree of life, and so we were given life.
We left behind the way guarded by the cherub, and we rose up to heaven. We became immortal and near to God.
As for wine, I think my word is unnecessary, because it is nothing at all to monks. The apostle Paul showed it to be the root and cause of defilement, and said:
"Do not get drunk with wine, in which is defilement." Wine is a deadly poison, the mother of evil desires, and what stirs them up.
In the end an evil harvest comes from evil seed. Hate it, and do not accept these things even for one moment.
It stripped the patriarchs naked, not through gluttony but through inexperience. It is wine that makes the eyes bloodshot, reddens the complexion, and turns a handsome face ugly.
What do you have to do with that evil lover? If you do not put it away from you, its deceit will soon show itself in you.
My brethren, do not think little of yourselves, as if you were transient and perishable things. The power that knows itself
knows all things. So you should know that we are beings created immortal and imperishable, beyond all other created things,
honored above the visible things with an existence that has no end. For this reason it is right that we guard ourselves and take care for the sake of the life to come.
In our small humanity he created this vast world again, and he made it greater than the world by giving it a speaking and rational soul.
He gave it a fulfilment that has a beginning but no end: an immortal soul.
In this way he brought us near to the nature of the angels, while our other part is like the perishable animals.
A human being is neither an angel nor a beast, but something between them, a creature of another kind made from both:
He joined that one being together from soul and flesh, set it in a place of battle and victory, and gave it the power of self-rule,
and he placed it at the point of balance of the scales and of its own mind. For this mind goes out between the two united natures, and it is the one that governs.
If it somehow leans upward, it brings [the flesh] to the spiritual nature and makes the will of the flesh obey it, and this draws [?] it toward immortality and life.
And if it leans downward and brings the soul to the will of the flesh, it makes it a slave to death and corruption. We have these two wills, opposed to each other, as the apostle says:
"The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, and they attack each other." And again he says:
"I do not do what I want, but I do what I hate. If not that [?], I bear witness to the law that it is good.
So now it is no longer I who do this, but what dwelt in me: the sin that is in me.
For I agree with the law of God, and I see another law in my members that fights against it."
You see how clearly the apostle tells us about the two wills that oppose each other and fight:
One will is natural and created. Adam had it before he transgressed the commandment in Paradise, while he was still spiritual, and Nathanael [?]. But the other one
settled in us after the error, not by nature: it broke in [?] from outside the heart by cunning.
For this reason the apostle did not say that it is created sin, which fights against the law of my mind.
Understand from these words, brothers: if any of you gives in to those opposing forces,
that person is taken captive by that hateful will. But if he does not put to death the deeds of the flesh, he lives spiritually without willing it [?].
So now it has been shown that both these wills are in our power, even though the devil's will keeps pulling its own evil will toward the desires of the flesh, without rest.
But the same apostle says: "What the law could not do, because it was weak through the flesh,
"God sent his Son in the likeness of flesh," and he took on this flesh of ours without sin,
cleansed of all the error of the first Adam, so that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us,
"for the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life."
And truly the mind of the flesh is death, for its thoughts urge us toward every kind of impurity.
It is not only an enemy outside, but one that is with you always, when you lie down and when you rise up, in all your actions.
Guard against it as much as you can, so that it does not [?] you with a stone. It calls to you without mercy, as an enemy does [?].
But I want you to put it under the bridle of the spiritual will, so that in this way you return to that first created state to which our Lord has brought us back, for you were created great.
If somehow you keep it and do not fall to that lower place, then, since you share in the wisdom of God,
how much is possible for the creature together with the Creator! You are living, like the angels, and mortal, like the animals; lower than the lowest of the abysses and higher than the highest,
so that you are beyond grasping: greater than all great things and smaller than all small things, and immortal within mortality.
This is your creation in two parts. That is why it is wondrous: it is the craftsmanship of the Worker of wonders.
One of the saints, who spoke with great depth, marveled at this wondrous mixture and wished to separate himself from something.
He cast off what he saw as lacking and powerless, and then he lamented and spoke thus:
"O, how I was joined to it I do not know, nor how I am the image of God and yet mingled with clay. When it is healthy, it [?] (rises up against me), and when it is brought low, there is grief.
"I love it as my companion, for it is a servant, and I turn away from it as from an enemy. I flee from it as from a curse, and I am ashamed of it [?] as of a fellow-dweller.
"I want to waste it away, and yet I have no other helper toward the good. From it I need tears, from it fasting,
"vigils, from it the offering of prayer and many good labors, which are not possible without the body.
"For I know what I exist for, and it is fitting for me to rise up to the works of my God.
"I would shun it, yet it is my fellow-worker, and I do not know how to escape its assault, so that I may not be weighed down by the fetter
"that drags me down to earth, and so fall away from God. It is a cheerful enemy and a false friend.
"O union and separation! What I fear, I shelter; what I love, I fear. Before the battle I make peace, and before making peace I wage war."
For this reason He made us so: that through the [?] (hardness/struggle) and warfare of this flesh we might look to humility, so that this feeble teaching of rule might be gathered together [?],
so that you may know that we are both high and low, dwellers of light or of darkness, wherever [the will] inclines.
This is our mixture: when we are exalted by the image, we are made small because of the earth. You have understood your union and your inner war.
Hold yourself unbending in every way; do not cling to pleasure and evil intent.
And see that you have another enemy too, who cast you down from on high and never plans anything good for you.
And he aids the will of the flesh, that bodiless Pharaoh, who was changed from light into darkness, against the enlightened man who has passed through the Jordan.
He seizes him with his own host, the thickness of his darkness, and forces those created free to be his slaves,
so that he may carry them off to Babylon, to that hell which devours many, which has been sunk in the wall [?] (or sea) of fire by the coming of Christ our God,
who was born of the Virgin, the second Adam, with the nature of the first Adam but without sin.
But those who have enlightened themselves from that same beginningless Light [?] (rested/were refreshed) in delight and remained unerring in joy,
fastened with zeal to that immortal life close at hand, in the love of that same enlightening Light, forever.
And when they had received these and many other teachings, he said to them:
"Go and strengthen the flocks of Christ." And he sent some of them toward Kakheti and some toward Kukheti,
some to the upper part of the country, one to Gareji [?] (or: to the outlying parts), and others to the area around this royal city of ours.
But they went off and settled, some in groves and some on mountains, in caves and holes in the ground.
People came to them from every side and were edified by their words and by the deeds done through them, and through them the multitude of believers was strengthened.
Holy John had brought with him at his coming a very great number of relics of the holy martyrs, and he kept them before his eyes.
He looked on them as more precious than all treasures, as though many hosts were standing around him. He placed his hope in them and was comforted by them.
And truly they were great treasures, more precious than all gems: the bones of the martyrs, of the brave warriors who were invincible in the contest,
who shed their blood for him who bought us with his own blood, the bulwarks of the human race.
Whoever was in distress fled to them, and they ran to them rejoicing; people on land and people at sea alike called on them for help.
Father John kept those relics of the saints before him as if he were watching the day of their contest. In this way he talked with them and lived through the torments of each one in his own mind.
Every day he made a martyr of himself and added to his labours. He prayed to them and kissed them with great longing.
Once, when he was sending out his disciples, he gave them some of the relics of the holy martyrs,

so that they would have them as a protection for their heads, and so that they would build churches in the name of each of the martyrs in the dwellings that were being prepared for them by the grace of God.
The blessed elder lived alone on that mountain with only one servant of theirs [?], in great ascetic struggle. His prayer rose up to heaven, purified the air and passed through the ether.
But the demons, those haters of good, who had lived on that mountain from of old,
could not endure the prayers and supplications of our father John, because these pierced them like red-hot arrows.
One day all those powers of darkness rose up. They attacked holy John, as it were, and began to fight against him with many devices.
They raged around him and tried to frighten him. They assailed him day and night, as though they had some power, and threatened to throw him down from that rock.
But the blessed elder armed himself with the cross of Christ and counted their phantoms as nothing. He said to them: "Here I am, if you have received permission."
One day the whole multitude rose up and appeared openly. They surrounded blessed John and said to him: "Why have you come here?"
One of them, the chief of the demons, called him by name: "John, why are you contending with us? Where have you come from? This place is ours, and you cannot stay here.
Do you not know that this boldness of yours toward us will destroy you completely? You cannot stand against this whole multitude, so do not deceive yourself."
Blessed John answered them: "You have never had any good intention toward our race. So how should I listen to you?
Your place is darkness: flee there!" And at once that great multitude fled, by the power of Christ.
O listener, was it not you who took that place from me, the paradise of delight? It was mine, and you devised a scheme like this against Adam and drove him out of it [?].
And there was a time when we became food for death through your schemes. But God could not endure the complete dishonouring of his own image,
but he came and found it buried in the depth, and raised it up, renewed it, and healed all the wounds you had inflicted.
And behold, today you are driven out on every side by his offspring, for those gifts have spread through the whole world, and there is no place left for you except darkness,
just as you, of your own will, hated the light and loved the darkness. For you were an angel and became a fallen one; you were one who praised, and you were made an accuser.
But we shall receive in full that place which was promised through your deceit, and behold, from this dwelling we shall pass over to heaven.
With pitiful voices they said: "Woe to us, for the invoking of the name of Jesus drives us out of every place,
and gives power to those who follow him. Let us go, then, and settle there among the more remote pagans."

And at once, like a thick mist and darkness, they came out of that mountain, became invisible, and went off toward the north. And blessed John gave thanks to God when he saw their fall and destruction.
All who lived around that mountain heard of this event and saw the glorious wonder of God the wonderworker that had taken place
through the prayer of our father John, who fulfils the will of those who fear him.
For they had known beforehand the wickedness of the demons who had dwelt in that place, and they glorified God.
And the blessed elder lived on that mountain alone and was served by his own disciple.
Day by day he renewed himself and strove not to appear empty-handed before his Lord, but brought good works before him as gifts every day.
For this mountain was formerly without water, and no water at all could be found anywhere around it, although the former pagans who had lived in the tower had made many efforts,
for they could not bring up water even by hard digging in that dry ground.
And blessed John saw the great labours of his disciple, how he would carry water up from the foot of the mountain and bring it up for the elder's use.
For that place is a steep ascent on every side and a long climb. And the elder took pity on his disciple Elijah, and he prayed and besought his Lord to give him water close by.
Then he who gave water in the desert to his people Israel by the hand of Moses his servant, and brought forth rivers from the dry rock by the striking of the staff,
and rescued the twelve tribes, the sons of Israel, that great camp, not once or twice but many times, as the apostle Paul says:
"For they drank from the spiritual rock which they followed, and that rock was Christ."
That rock was a figure of Christ, and the staff a shadow of the cross.
And since the blessed one too followed Christ in all things, Christ heard his prayer, and at his entreaty it happened at once, at the place where the cross of Christ had been set up.
And just as Moses struck with the staff, so he, using the cross in place of the staff, struck that dry ground where no one had ever seen any water at all, and sweet water gushed out.

And when this great miracle took place, people came from every side to see it, for the inhabitants of the surrounding area knew that there had been no water in that place.
And by his holy grace the spring became not only something for everyday use, but many healings also took place there.
People brought the sick with all kinds of illnesses, and those possessed by demons, and all who anointed themselves from that spring were healed.
And he drove it away to a distant land. And those who come in faith receive benefit from it to this very day.
But he did not wish to build anything in that place. Instead he lived as the rule of the solitary life requires: he had found a small cave in a cleft of the rock,
and in it he completed the pilgrimage of this faithful life, "first in great want, afflicted, of whom this world was not worthy," and so on.
And as the Lord multiplied miracles through him, word of him spread through the land of Kartli, and he shone out like the morning star.
he who had glorified God in secret. Through him [Kartli] widened its bosom and received that great light brought down from on high,
For it was not possible for anyone to light a lamp and hide it under a bushel; it is set on a lampstand to give light to people.
Even when such men wish to hide themselves, it is like a perfumer who fills a flask with fragrance, puts it inside another vessel, seals it well, and hangs it up to carry wherever he wishes.
The perfumer thinks that he is keeping it hidden, but the fragrance of the ointment reaches everyone who comes near.
In the same way good deeds cannot be hidden, even if those who do them do not wish them to be known.
One day his servant, the blessed Elijah the deacon, went to the God-given spring to fetch water.
There, beside the spring, stood a great and very terrible bear. The blessed Elijah was badly frightened, turned back, and told the great John.
John came and said to the bear: "If you have not yet drunk that water, drink and be on your way." And he laid a law upon it and said:
"In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ I tell you: from now on you shall have no power to do evil or harm to the people you meet on this mountain."
And when the beast received the command from the elder, it unlearned how to harm anyone.
It went on its way, and kept looking back as if at a friend speaking sweetly to it. It bowed its head and quietly showed the bearing of obedience.
And its beastly nature entirely [?]; nor did it show any sign of fleeing, for it had changed its own wickedness and been turned to good.
And through the prayer of that holy man, to this day it walks along with whoever it meets, like a gentle sheep.
This is not surprising, for even beasts know how to show honour; they look to those who rule [?] and to the light.
He who fell into the pit among the beasts and shut the mouths of the lions, which had long been deprived of food and were very hungry,
lay among them like an unbreakable adamant stone, and the beasts did not dare to touch him at all.
Instead they came up and licked his feet, as if saying: "This is not the flesh that is meant to be our food,"
since he would not consent to taste the dishes from the royal table, but only seeds. This man ate no bread and drank no water for three weeks.
It is right for us to learn from this the honour paid to those who fast.
But the blessed elder, through his own severe labour of fasting, did not undertake merely to keep that flesh-eating beast away from himself alone.
Rather, it was sent like an apostle to its own kind, its kin and companions, and to the offspring of their offspring [?], so that they would harm no one.
And that commandment became a bridle [?] for them and softened their teeth. To this very day they live on that mountain and harm no one.
I was ashamed and grieved when I heard this as well: how that beastly nature, dumb and senseless, obeyed the word of the saints,
while we have shown ourselves more wicked than the beasts. We read of what happened among them [?], and we hear the commandments that were given, and yet we do not stop harming our neighbours.
We abstain from eating meat, yet we chew the flesh of our neighbour. If only we were at least like those beasts, and not like flesh-
eating men! We have received a commandment from God to love our neighbour as ourselves,
but we have hated him along with ourselves, for hatred of one's neighbour is hatred of oneself, and the deceiver who brings this about is envy.
O envious one, turn away from envy. Envy is death; flee from it, so that you may not die.
Do not envy those who advance in virtue, and confess that you are envious. Envy is praised [?]: that love which is for death [?].
This, for the sake of life, a deliverer and [?], which ruins the minds of those who plot it [?]. Instead, hold fast [?] to the Scriptures and find deliverance,
and imitate those who have been made perfect in virtue. Do not envy, so that you may escape the snare of the enemy, if only a little [?].
And let me return again to the point where I left off [?].
